summary: Teach the digestive system to 7–9s as the journey one mouthful takes through a single long tube, with a distinct job at each stop: mouth (teeth break food up, saliva starts to soften it), oesophagus (a squeezing tube pushing food down), stomach (churns food with acid into mush), small intestine (the long coiled tube where nutrients cross into the blood), and large intestine (removes water from the leftovers, forming waste). The two things children must take away are the ORDER of the organs and the KEY job at each — especially that nutrients are absorbed into the blood at the small intestine (a hook to circulation) and that waste and water are handled by the large intestine. Make the surprising facts physical: the intestines are metres long, coiled up; the stomach is a stretchy bag, not where 'poo is made'; muscles — not gravity — push food along.
misconceptions: 'The stomach digests everything / is where it all happens' — missing that most nutrient absorption is in the small intestine.
'Food goes to the stomach and waste comes straight out' — skipping the long intestines and the absorption and water-removal steps.
'There are two tubes — one for food, one for wee' — confusing the digestive tract with the urinary system; digestion is one continuous food tube.
'The stomach is where poo is made' — waste is formed in the large intestine after nutrients and water are removed.
'Digestion means food dissolving into nothing' — missing that useful nutrients are absorbed into the blood and the rest becomes waste.
'The intestines are short' — not appreciating they are several metres long, coiled up inside the belly.
'Gravity moves food down' — not knowing muscles squeeze food along (you can swallow upside down).

activities.title: Follow your food: tracing one mouthful through the tube
steps: Trace the path of one mouthful out loud and in order — mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine — naming the ONE main job at each stop.
Map the journey onto your own torso with your hands as you narrate, so the sequence becomes a remembered story rather than a labelled diagram.

At the small intestine, describe the moment of insight: the useful nutrients pass THROUGH the gut wall INTO the blood, which carries them around the body (for example to the leg muscles); only the leftovers travel on.
At the large intestine, describe water being drawn back out and the remainder forming waste.
Replay the journey yourself, narrating the order and each job without prompts, to check it holds together.
activities.insight: Digestion is not food 'vanishing in the stomach' — it is an ordered sequence that extracts nutrients into the blood at a specific place (the small intestine), while the large intestine deals with water and waste.

activities.title: How long are the intestines really?
steps: Unroll roughly a 7-metre length of string or rope to represent the intestines, then coil it into a small space to show how they pack into the belly.
Compare this length against your own height and against the small 'tummy' many children imagine.
Explain in your own words why 'the tummy is one small bag' is wrong — the gut is a very long, coiled tube.
activities.insight: The intestines are several metres long and coiled up inside the belly, not short — this corrects the idea that digestion happens in one small bag.

activities.title: Hands-on models of the mechanical steps
steps: Mash a cracker with a little water inside a sealed bag to model how the stomach churns food with acid into a mush.
Push a small soft object along inside a length of tights/stocking to model how muscles squeeze food along the tube (peristalsis).

Say that both models show physical breaking-down and moving (churning, squeezing), then name the chemical help in the real body that the models do not show (saliva, stomach acid and other digestive juices), so digestion is understood as both, not as magic.
activities.insight: Digestion involves physical breakdown and movement driven by teeth and muscle action, plus chemical help from saliva, stomach acid and digestive juices — food is actively worked on, not simply dissolved into nothing.

activities.title: Explain-the-journey diagnostic: apple to leg muscle
steps: Answer: 'After you eat an apple, some of it ends up helping your leg muscles work, and some comes out later as waste. How does a bit of the apple get all the way from inside your tummy to your leg? Talk me through the journey and explain how the useful part gets there.'
Point to WHERE the useful part leaves the gut and enters the blood.
Say whether the large intestine absorbs nutrients too, or does a different job, and name that job.
activities.insight: Only a learner who grasps absorption into the blood can bridge gut to muscle; stating where nutrients cross and distinguishing the large intestine's water-and-waste job shows real understanding.

activities.title: One shared food tube, not two pipes
steps: Explain that the digestive tract is ONE continuous food tube from mouth to the end — not a separate pipe for food and another for drink.

Say that water travels along the same tube as food and is absorbed through the intestine walls (much of it in the small intestine, with the large intestine drawing back the remaining water from the leftovers), rather than imagining it carried by a second internal pipe.
Correct the idea that 'the stomach is where poo is made' by naming the large intestine as where waste is formed, after nutrients and water have been removed.
activities.insight: Digestion happens in one continuous tract; waste is formed in the large intestine, not the stomach, and there is no second internal food/drink pipe.

checkQuestion: After you eat an apple, some of it ends up helping your leg muscles work, and some of it comes out later as waste. How does a bit of the apple get all the way from inside your tummy to your leg? Talk me through the journey and explain how the useful part gets there.
checkAnswer: As the apple moves through the gut it is broken down; in the small intestine the useful nutrients pass THROUGH the gut wall INTO the blood, and the blood carries them around the body to places like the leg muscles. The leftover waste carries on into the large intestine, where water is removed, and leaves as faeces. The key idea is that nutrients cross out of the gut into the blood — food doesn't just run through one tube and come straight out.
